extracted.intended_audience: writers (especially children's/YA) and allies interested in writing or publishing LGBTQ+/queer fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what counts as LGBTQ+ (queer) fiction and best practices for creating respectful, three-dimensional queer representation across genres, with specific notes for children's and YA writers. Covers definitional questions, character criteria (Vito Russo Test), authorship, craft, and representation ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of LGBTQ+ fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: LGBTQ+ fiction = fiction about or by queer people that explicitly or implicitly explores LGBTQ+ experiences, issues, relationships, history or pride
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There isn’t one single definition, but this working definition frames the rest of the article: focus is on fiction that is about or by queer people and that explores queer-related experiences or themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: A story does not need to be about being queer
rubrics_metrics.description: Does an LGBTQ+ story need to be about being queer? No — it doesn’t need to be specifically about being queer, but it definitely can be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some fiction explicitly explores coming out, identity, and challenges; other stories include queer characters incidentally where sexuality/gender is not the plot focus. Both explicit and implicit inclusion are valid and implicit approaches help present queerness as commonplace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queer protagonist not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Does an LGBTQ+ story need to have a queer protagonist? No, it doesn’t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially in children’s fiction there are many books where a protagonist’s family member (parent, sibling) is queer; such books can still be considered LGBTQ+ fiction even if the protagonist themself is not queer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vito Russo Test — identifiable queer character
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a character who is identifiably lesbian, gay, bisexual and/or transgender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the first explicit Vito Russo Test criterion (from GLAAD) adapted to fiction: a queer presence must be clear enough to be recognized as part of the story’s representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vito Russo Test — character defined by more than orientation/gender
rubrics_metrics.description: The character must be defined by more than just their sexual orientation or gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The queer character should have unique traits and individuality—avoid one-dimensional depiction where sexuality/gender is their only defining trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vito Russo Test — character central to the story
rubrics_metrics.description: The character must be so central to the story that removing them would have a significant impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GLAAD notes the character should not be present merely to provide colorful commentary, urban authenticity, or a punchline; they should ‘matter’ to plot and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single queer character may classify a book as LGBTQ+ if they pass the Vito Russo Test
rubrics_metrics.description: Is a book considered LGBTQ+ if it has just one queer character? It can be argued yes IF that character meets the Vito Russo Test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the sole queer character is tokenistic or stereotypical (e.g., gay best friend/hairdresser used for comic/colour), the book should not be marketed as meaningful LGBTQ+ representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tokenism and stereotypes; make queer characters three-dimensional
rubrics_metrics.description: Queer characters must be believable, three-dimensional people and not token additions or stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of anti-patterns: characters who exist only to set up jokes or to add ‘authenticity’ without real depth. Replace stereotypes with distinct personalities, motives, histories, and roles in the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer multiple LGBTQ+ characters to reflect diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s often advisable to have more than one LGBTQ+ character in a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple queer characters allow celebration of many identities under the rainbow, reduce the risk of one character representing an entire community, and more realistically reflect societal diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer identity is not a requirement but responsibility matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Does a writer have to be queer to write an LGBTQ+ story? No — anyone can write queer stories provided they are committed to writing respectfully and informedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable authors include out queer writers, closeted queer writers, people exploring identity, and committed allies. However, writers without personal experience should research thoroughly and consider hiring sensitivity readers to avoid harmful portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: LGBTQ+ is not a genre; queer content can appear across genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Is LGBTQ+ a genre? No — genre refers to style (romance, sci‑fi, fantasy, mystery), and LGBTQ+ is a thematic/content descriptor that can be written within any genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reach readers, include queer characters across genres (queer romance, queer fantasy, queer mystery, etc.); don’t conflate queer content with a specific set of genre conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core craft elements remain essential
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to queer-specific considerations, writers must attend to usual craft elements (protagonist goal, stakes, conflict, arc of change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good representation alone doesn’t make a compelling story — ensure the protagonist has clear goals, meaningful stakes, conflict, and an arc so the queer elements are embedded in strong storytelling.
